title.en: Autumn Leaves in Seoul's Palaces, Namsan and Parks: Where and When to Go

summary.en: Where autumn color is best in Seoul's palaces, on Namsan and in Seoul Forest, when it usually peaks, how the 2026 free palace entry works, and a half-day route.

guide.audience: Visitors in Seoul between late October and mid-November who want autumn color at the palaces, on Namsan or in a city park, and need to plan around tickets, closing days and crowds.
guide.method: Researched from the official sources listed below, checked on October 25, 2026. Foliage forecasts are estimates and hours, fees and booking rules can change; the linked official pages are the final word.
guide.quickAnswer: Central Seoul usually colors from late October into early or mid-November, a little after Bukhansan, whose average peak is October 28; the first week of November is the safest bet. For one walk, book Changdeokgung's Secret Garden, then add Changgyeonggung's pond and Deoksugung's stone-wall road at dusk. Palace admission is free from October 29 to November 15, 2026, but the Secret Garden still needs a paid, timed ticket.

en.heading: Why the city center turns later than the mountains
paragraphs: Seoul gets its autumn color in two waves, and most disappointment comes from confusing them. The first wave is on the mountains. The Korea Meteorological Administration (KMA) tracks Bukhansan (북한산), the granite massif on the city's northern edge, and records first color when about a fifth of the mountain has turned from the summit down, and the peak when about 80 percent has. Its 1991–2020 averages put Bukhansan's first color on October 15 and its peak on October 28. In 2026 the first color arrived on October 14, a day ahead of the average.

The second wave is in the city itself: palace gardens, park groves and the ginkgo trees that line downtown streets. Nobody forecasts a palace pond, so treat the national outlooks as a frame. The Korea Forest Service's 2026 forecast, issued on September 22, puts the national peak, defined as half of a tree's leaves turned, at October 30 for ginkgo and October 31 for maples and oaks, slightly later than the five-year average. A foliage map released on October 8 by the Korea Tourism Organization and the Korea National Arboretum expects the Seoul metropolitan area to peak from late October.

Downtown trees usually lag behind the mountain. When Seoul published its list of autumn walking roads in October 2025, it expected the Bukhansan area to peak around October 25 and the city center from the end of October into early or mid-November. Our reading for 2026: between October 28 and November 12 the palaces should show strong color, and the first week of November is the safest bet for maples and street ginkgo together. After mid-November the show thins fast, and one night of wind and rain can strip a ginkgo avenue.

en.heading: Changdeokgung's Secret Garden: book this one first
paragraphs: If you can take only one autumn walk in Seoul, make it the Huwon (후원), the royal garden behind Changdeokgung (창덕궁). Its maples grow in folded valleys around ponds and small pavilions that were placed where the views already were, so the color frames architecture rather than a lawn. The square pond Buyongji, the lotus pond Aeryeonji and the pond Gwallamji lie on the standard route. The walk involves real slopes and unpaved earth that turns slick after rain. Our Changdeokgung guide reads the garden building by building.

Entry is only by timed session, and autumn is when sessions sell out. Each language session takes 100 people: 50 tickets go on sale online at 10:00 Korea time six days ahead, and 50 are sold at the palace ticket office from 09:00 on the day. In November, English sessions start at 10:30, 11:30, 14:30 and 15:30; from December the 15:30 session is dropped. The garden ticket costs 5,000 won for adults. From November, Changdeokgung keeps winter hours of 09:00 to 17:30, with last entry at 16:30, and it closes on Mondays.

One trap catches visitors every year: free palace weeks do not include the garden. From October 29 to November 15, 2026, Changdeokgung's halls are free, but the Huwon keeps its paid, timed ticket, so book it exactly as you would in any other week. Skip the garden if stairs and uneven ground are a problem or if you cannot commit to a fixed time. Changgyeonggung next door gives you maples without either constraint.

en.heading: Changgyeonggung's pond and Gyeongbokgung's island pavilion
paragraphs: Changgyeonggung (창경궁) shares a wall with Changdeokgung, and a connecting gate, Hamyangmun (함양문), lets you walk from one to the other. Its pond, Chundangji (춘당지), is the most relaxed foliage spot among the palaces: no booking, open ground around the water and maples leaning over the banks. The palace normally opens from 09:00 to 21:00, with last entry at 20:00, which makes it the place to watch the color fade into lamplight. One exception in 2026: from November 10 to 15, daytime visits end at 17:30 while a separately booked night program uses the grounds.

At Gyeongbokgung (경복궁), walk north past the throne hall to Hyangwonjeong (향원정), the small two-story hexagonal pavilion on an island in a square pond, reached by the wooden bridge Chwihyanggyo (취향교). King Gojong added it to his private garden in the 1870s, and in a good year the maples on the bank turn the water red around it. A restoration finished in 2021 moved the bridge back to the island's north side, so older photographs show it facing the other way.

Gyeongbokgung closes on Tuesdays, and from November 1 it switches to winter hours, 09:00 to 17:00 with last entry at 16:00, so the warm late light is short. It is also the busiest palace. Go at opening and head straight for the pond before the tour groups arrive, then come back to the throne hall. The front courtyards look much the same at 11:00 as at 09:00; the pond does not.

en.heading: Namsan: mountain color without leaving the center
paragraphs: Namsan (남산) gives you mountain foliage inside the city. Its slopes carry mixed woodland, the Joseon-era city wall, Hanyangdoseong (한양도성), runs along its ridge, and N Seoul Tower stands at the top. Seoul lists Namsan Park among its autumn walking roads partly because its park roads carry no ordinary traffic, so you can follow the curves without dodging cars. Color here tends to follow the city center more than Bukhansan, which makes Namsan a good substitute on a day when the palace you wanted is closed.

Choose your direction by the light. Walking up from Namsangol Hanok Village in mid-afternoon puts the sun behind the maples as you climb, and you reach the summit for the long view over a city turning gold and gray at once. If your knees prefer it, ride up and walk down instead. Our Namsangol and Namsan guide gives the bus routes, the cable car and the official city-wall section, so you can pick the version that suits you.

Namsan is the wrong choice in haze or rain. Its appeal is the pairing of leaves and long views, and on a gray day you get damp stairs without either. Check the sky in the morning, and if visibility is poor, swap Namsan for Seoul Forest or a palace garden.

en.heading: Seoul Forest: ginkgo gold without a ticket
paragraphs: Seoul Forest (서울숲) opened in 2005 on almost 50 hectares beside the Han River, and the city lists it among its autumn walks for a grove of about 600 ginkgo trees. It is a different experience from the palaces: no ticket, no closing day, no timed session and room for children to run. The park is open 24 hours and free. Seoul Forest Station on the Suin-Bundang Line is about 240 meters away from Exits 3 and 4, and Ttukseom Station on Line 2 about 540 meters from Exit 8.

Ginkgo is a different kind of autumn from maple. The yellow arrives almost at once, holds for a short spell and then drops in a carpet, often after a windy night. Female trees also shed seeds whose fleshy coats smell strongly when crushed, so watch where you step. Seoul Forest is our pick for a Monday, when Changdeokgung, Changgyeonggung and Deoksugung are all closed, and for families who would rather picnic than queue.

The park also sits beside Seongsu-dong, the former factory district now packed with cafés and design shops, so a morning among the ginkgo turns easily into lunch. Walk the wooded paths first, while the light is low and the grove is quiet, and keep the riverside edge of the park for later. Unlike the palaces, the park has no closing hour, so an early start costs you nothing.

en.heading: Deoksugung and the stone-wall road after dark
paragraphs: Deoksugung (덕수궁) is the palace for people who have spent the day elsewhere. It stays open until 21:00, with last entry at 20:00, closes on Mondays and normally costs 1,000 won, and its trees glow under the lamps in a way the morning palaces never show you. It is compact: an hour inside is enough unless you also want the guided interior of Seokjojeon, the stone hall of Emperor Gojong's Korean Empire.

Outside the wall, the road that curves along Deoksugung's stone wall toward Jeongdong-gil (정동길) is one of Seoul's classic autumn streets. The city includes Jeongdong-gil in its list of autumn roads for its ginkgo trees set against modern-era buildings, and from the palace's main gate to the Jeongdong crossroads is a short stroll. Both are public streets, open at every hour, so the walk still works after the palace has closed.

Our judgment: this is the best autumn plan for an evening and a poor one for a morning. The gray stone and yellow leaves need low light to look their best, and the palace grounds are calmer after 18:00 than at noon. Pair it with dinner near City Hall, and save it for the end of a day built around the other palaces.

en.heading: Free entry, crowds and when to be where
paragraphs: From October 29 to November 15, 2026, admission is free for everyone at Gyeongbokgung, Changdeokgung, Changgyeonggung, Deoksugung, Jongmyo and the Joseon royal tombs during the Korea Grand Festival. Regular closing days still apply: Gyeongbokgung and Jongmyo close on Tuesdays and the other palaces on Mondays. The Secret Garden keeps its paid, timed tickets, and Jongmyo opens for self-guided visits on every open day of the period.

Free entry and peak color together bring the heaviest palace crowds of the year, especially on the three weekends inside the period. Three habits help. Arrive at 09:00, when the gates open, and go to the garden or pond before the courtyards. Put Gyeongbokgung and the Secret Garden on weekdays. And save Changgyeonggung and Deoksugung, the two palaces open until 21:00, for late afternoon, when the day visitors thin out.

Two calendar details are worth knowing. Every Wednesday is already a free Culture Day at the palaces except Gyeongbokgung and the Secret Garden, so the free period changes weekends far more than midweek days. And the period ends on Sunday, November 15, about when downtown color usually starts to fade; from November 16 normal fees return, 3,000 won at Gyeongbokgung and Changdeokgung and 1,000 won at Changgyeonggung and Deoksugung.

en.heading: Photographing leaves without becoming the obstacle
paragraphs: Palace rules are relaxed about ordinary photography: visitors' souvenir photos count as permitted. Commercial shoots for film, drama or advertising need a paid permit, character costumes and similar props need separate permission, and drone filming is limited to approved public-interest work, so leave the drone at the hotel. Staff can also restrict photography in particular spots to prevent crowding, which tends to happen at exactly the ponds this guide sends you to.

The rest is courtesy. Stay on paths and outside ropes, because closed areas need permission to enter. Do not shake branches for a falling-leaf shot or sweep leaves into piles; others are waiting for the same tree. The rules do not ban tripods outright, but on a narrow pond edge one blocks a whole line of people, so set it up only when the path is empty. In the Secret Garden, keep up with your group and step aside to shoot. And treat people in hanbok as fellow visitors, not props: ask before a close portrait.

For the pictures themselves, mornings give still water and reflections at Hyangwonjeong and Chundangji, while afternoon sun shining through maples gives the glowing red that photographs best. Shade under palace eaves is deep, so expose for the leaves rather than the roofs. In November the palaces that close early shut before the best evening light, one more reason to end the day at Deoksugung.

en.heading: A half-day route for peak week
paragraphs: This version works from Tuesday to Sunday and takes about five hours. Six days ahead, at 10:00 Korea time, book the 10:30 English session of the Secret Garden. On the day, reach Changdeokgung at 09:00 from Anguk Station on Line 3 and spend an hour among the halls. At 10:30 join the garden session. Around midday, walk through Hamyangmun into Changgyeonggung for 40 minutes at Chundangji, then leave for lunch toward Jongno.

In the afternoon, take the subway or a taxi to City Hall and enter Deoksugung around 15:00. Walk the grounds as the light lowers, then leave by the main gate and follow the stone-wall road to Jeongdong-gil before dark. The only fixed appointment in the day is the garden session; everything else can slide by half an hour without harm.

On a Monday, when those three palaces close, switch the order: Gyeongbokgung at 09:00 and straight to Hyangwonjeong, then Seoul Forest for ginkgo in the afternoon. On a Tuesday, run the main route and add Namsan at the end instead of the evening walk if the sky is clear. If you have only one evening, skip the rest and go to Deoksugung from 17:00, then the stone-wall road.

faq.q: When is the best week to see autumn leaves in Seoul's palaces?
faq.a: In most years, the first week of November. Bukhansan on the city's edge peaks first, with a KMA average of October 28, and palace gardens and street ginkgo downtown usually follow from the end of October into early or mid-November. The Korea Forest Service's 2026 forecast put the national peak at October 30 for ginkgo and October 31 for maples.

faq.q: Is the Secret Garden free during the October 29 to November 15 free-entry period?
faq.a: No. The free period covers palace admission at Changdeokgung, but the Huwon garden keeps its paid, timed tickets: 5,000 won for adults, with half of each session sold online from 10:00 six days ahead and half at the ticket office from 09:00 on the day. Book it as early as you would in any other autumn week.

faq.q: Where can I see autumn leaves in the evening?
faq.a: Deoksugung and Changgyeonggung stay open until 21:00, with last entry at 20:00, and both close on Mondays. In 2026 Changgyeonggung's visits end at 17:30 from November 10 to 15. The stone-wall road outside Deoksugung and Jeongdong-gil are public streets you can walk at any hour.

faq.q: What should I change if it rains during peak foliage?
faq.a: Light rain deepens the color and empties the palaces, so keep a palace plan and wear shoes with grip for the Secret Garden's slopes. Strong wind and heavy rain can strip ginkgo trees overnight, so if a storm is forecast, see Seoul Forest or the stone-wall road before it arrives. Drop Namsan on a day of low cloud.

faq.q: If I have time for only one palace in autumn, which should it be?
faq.a: Changdeokgung, if you can book the Secret Garden: its valleys of maples are the finest autumn walk in Seoul. Without a garden ticket, choose Changgyeonggung for its pond and evening hours, or Gyeongbokgung if you also want the throne hall and the Hyangwonjeong pavilion, remembering that it closes on Tuesdays.

title.en: Deoksugung and Jeong-dong: A Walk Through Korea's Short-Lived Empire

summary.en: Deoksugung's imperial halls, the stone-wall road, Jungmyeongjeon, the Russian legation tower and Jeong-dong's mission buildings, with hours, tours and a walking order.

guide.audience: Visitors who want to understand the Korean Empire of 1897 to 1910 on foot, combining Deoksugung's halls with the buildings of the surrounding Jeong-dong neighborhood in a half day.
guide.method: Researched from the official sources listed below, checked on October 25, 2026. Hours, fees, tours and ceremony times can change; the linked official pages are the final word.
guide.quickAnswer: Start at Daehanmun for the 11:00 guard ceremony, see Junghwajeon and the stone hall Seokjojeon inside Deoksugung, then walk the stone-wall road to Jeongdong-gil, Jungmyeongjeon and the Russian legation tower. Allow about four hours. The palace opens 09:00 to 21:00 and closes on Mondays; Seokjojeon is entered only on guided sessions, with English at 11:50 and 14:50.

en.heading: 1897: why an emperor chose a cramped palace
paragraphs: Deoksugung (덕수궁) began as an emergency. In 1593, with the capital's palaces burned during the Japanese invasion, King Seonjo held court in the private manor of Grand Prince Wolsan, and in 1611 King Gwanghae made it an official palace named Gyeongungung (경운궁). For almost three centuries afterward it was a minor palace. What made it matter was the neighborhood that grew up around it in the 1880s and 1890s, when Western legations and missions settled in Jeong-dong (정동).

On February 11, 1896, months after the assassination of his queen, King Gojong slipped away to the Russian legation on the hill behind the palace and governed from there for a year. On February 20, 1897 he returned not to Gyeongbokgung but to Gyeongungung, and later that year he proclaimed the Korean Empire, 대한제국 (Daehan Jeguk), with himself as emperor. Our reading: a palace surrounded by foreign legations was a choice as much as a necessity, a court placing itself in full view of the powers it hoped would guarantee its independence.

The empire lasted 13 years. A great fire destroyed many buildings in 1904; Japan forced Gojong to abdicate in 1907, after which the palace was renamed Deoksugung; and under colonial rule from 1910 it shrank, lost most of its halls and was folded into a public park project. What survives is a fragment, which is why the streets outside the walls are as much a part of this story as the palace itself.

en.heading: Daehanmun and Junghwajeon: the ceremonial front
paragraphs: You enter through Daehanmun (대한문), the main gate facing City Hall. It was called Daeanmun until repairs in 1906 gave it its present name. In front of it, the Seoul Metropolitan Government stages a Royal Guard Changing Ceremony at 11:00 and 14:00 every day except Monday. Each performance lasts about 25 minutes, costs nothing, takes place outside the ticket gate and can be cancelled in bad weather, so arrive ten minutes early for a clear view from the plaza side.

Inside, a short path leads to Junghwajeon (중화전), the throne hall. It went up in 1902 as a two-story building modeled on Changdeokgung's throne hall, burned in the 1904 fire and was rebuilt as the single-story hall you see by 1906. Compare it with Gyeongbokgung's throne hall if you have seen that one: a lower roof in a tighter courtyard, built in a hurry by a court with little money and less room. The rank stones in the courtyard still mark where officials stood by grade.

Behind it, Jeukjodang (즉조당) served as the palace's main hall before Junghwajeon existed, and Hamnyeongjeon (함녕전) was Gojong's bedchamber. He died there on January 21, 1919, more than a decade after losing his throne. These traditional halls are modest, and their interest lies in what they witnessed rather than in their carpentry, so a few minutes at each is enough unless you are following a guide.

en.heading: Seokjojeon, Jeonggwanheon and the empire's Western face
paragraphs: The building that stops most visitors is Seokjojeon (석조전), a neoclassical stone hall designed by a British architect named Harding, begun in 1900 and finished in 1910, the year the empire ended. Gojong used it as an office and audience hall. In 1946 and 1947 it hosted the US–Soviet Joint Commission that met over Korea's future, and since 2014 it has housed the Daehan Empire History Museum (대한제국역사관).

Jeonggwanheon (정관헌), behind Hamnyeongjeon, is a pavilion that wraps a Korean-style building in a Western colonnade, with decorative railings of deer and pine motifs between slender columns. Guides like to say that Gojong drank coffee here with foreign diplomats; treat that as a popular story rather than documented fact. The building's real interest is how openly it mixes two architectural vocabularies. Nearby, Dondeokjeon (돈덕전), a rebuilt Western-style reception hall, now holds rotating exhibitions.

These interiors keep shorter hours than the grounds. Seokjojeon opens from 09:30 to 17:30 and can be entered only on a guided session, the last at 16:30. Dondeokjeon opens from 09:00 to 17:30, with last entry at 17:00, and it closes between exhibitions, so check the Deoksugung notice board at royal.khs.go.kr if it is the reason for your visit. After 17:30, plan on the grounds and on seeing these buildings from outside.

en.heading: Tickets, free days and the two English tours
paragraphs: Deoksugung opens from 09:00 to 21:00 every day except Monday, with last entry at 20:00. When a Monday is a public holiday the palace opens and closes on the next non-holiday instead. Adults aged 19 to 64 pay 1,000 won. Foreign visitors aged 18 and under or 65 and over enter free with proof of age, and so does anyone in qualifying hanbok. Every Wednesday is a free Culture Day, and in 2026 the heritage service made entry free for everyone from October 29 to November 15.

Two English tours run, and they are separate services. The free palace commentary starts at 10:45 and 13:30 from Tuesday to Sunday, takes about 45 minutes and needs no booking for groups of fewer than ten; meet at the information map about 10 meters inside Daehanmun. The Seokjojeon interior tour in English runs at 11:50 and 14:50. Online booking opens a week ahead, and both English sessions also take foreign visitors first come at the museum's information desk, up to 20 people, with a passport or alien registration card.

Watch two clashes. The 10:45 palace tour overlaps the 11:00 guard ceremony, so choose one or take the 13:30 tour. And Seokjojeon tours can be restricted from 13:30 to 16:30 on the last Wednesday of each month, when the hall hosts concerts. Entry to each session opens three minutes before it starts, and latecomers can be refused.

en.heading: The stone-wall road and its unlucky reputation
paragraphs: Back outside Daehanmun, face the gate and follow the wall to your left along Deoksugung-gil (덕수궁길), the road that runs beside the palace's stone wall. Seoul's tourism office points out that it is a one-way street that winds deliberately to slow traffic, with the roadway and the pavement at the same height, which is why it feels like a pedestrian lane even though cars still use it. In autumn its ginkgo trees turn yellow against the gray stone. Keep to the edge when you stop for photographs.

Seoul residents joke that couples who walk this road together will break up. The usual explanation points to the courts that once stood here: the Gyeongseong Family Court stood beside the road, on the site of today's Seoul City Hall annex, and the old Supreme Court building, now the Seoul Museum of Art, stood just above it. The story goes that for decades couples on their way to a divorce hearing walked exactly this route.

The full wall road runs about 1,100 meters around the palace, and for decades part of it was blocked by the British Embassy, which has held its site since 1883; Seoul began reopening that stretch in 2017. For this walk you need only the open section from Daehanmun past the art museum to the small rotary where Jeongdong-gil (정동길) begins. From there Jeongdong-gil winds on between churches, schools and embassies.

en.heading: Jungmyeongjeon, where the empire signed away its diplomacy
paragraphs: Up a short lane off Jeongdong-gil stands Jungmyeongjeon (중명전), a brick building with arcaded verandas that began as an imperial library called Suokheon (수옥헌). After the 1904 fire Gojong moved in, and in 1905 it was renamed Jungmyeongjeon. On November 17, 1905, under Japanese coercion, the treaty that stripped Korea of its diplomatic rights was signed here, the agreement Koreans call the Eulsa Treaty (을사늑약), using a word that marks it as forced.

In 1907 Gojong sent envoys from here in secret to the peace conference at The Hague to protest the treaty, and Japan used the mission as its pretext to force his abdication. The building reopened to the public in 2010 after restoration. It opens from 09:30 to 17:30, with last entry at 17:00, and it is small enough to see in half an hour. Search 중명전 in Naver Map or Kakao Map, because the lane entrance is easy to walk past.

If you visit only one building outside the palace walls, make it this one. Seokjojeon shows the empire as it wanted to be seen, a modern state receiving guests in a stone hall; Jungmyeongjeon is where that image failed. Seeing both on the same afternoon is the clearest history lesson Jeong-dong offers, and it explains why Koreans still treat this neighborhood as a place of memory rather than simply a pretty street.

en.heading: Gojong's Road and the Russian legation tower
paragraphs: From the stone-wall road, a gated lane of a little over 100 meters, Gojong's Road (고종의 길), climbs toward Jeong-dong Park. Seoul laid it out for the 120th anniversary of the 1896 refuge, which fell in 2016, and opened it in 2018. It runs between high walls, so walk it in daylight; if it is closed when you arrive, reach the park from Jeongdong-gil instead.

At the top, Jeong-dong Park holds what is left of the Russian legation: a white three-story tower on a small rise. The main building was destroyed during the Korean War. This is where Gojong lived and governed from February 1896 to February 1897, and it was from here that he returned to Gyeongungung to remake it as an imperial palace. In a map app, search 정동공원 (Jeong-dong Park) or 구 러시아공사관 (former Russian legation).

The tower itself takes five minutes. The point of the detour is to stand where a king spent a year as a guest of a foreign legation, a few hundred meters from the palace he then chose to rebuild. It makes the geography of the empire concrete in a way no museum panel does, and it is free and nearly always quiet.

en.heading: A red-brick church, a mission school and a courthouse turned museum
paragraphs: Jeongdong First Methodist Church (정동제일교회) was founded in 1885. Its red-brick Bethel Chapel, dedicated on December 26, 1897, is a simplified Gothic building that was enlarged in 1916 and 1926, wrecked in the Korean War and restored, and it is designated Historic Site No. 256. Korea's first pipe organ was installed inside. It is a working church, so look in quietly on a weekday and leave Sunday mornings to its congregation.

Nearby, the red-brick Appenzeller/Noble Memorial Museum occupies a 1916 building that was the east hall of Paichai Hakdang (배재학당), the school the American Methodist missionary Henry Appenzeller started in 1885. Along Jeongdong-gil, the National Jeongdong Theater (국립정동극장), opened in 1995, recalls Wongaksa, often described as Korea's first modern theater; our traditional performances guide covers its programs.

Up a short slope from the wall road, the Seoul Museum of Art (서울시립미술관) keeps the arched Renaissance-style facade of the 1928 Gyeongseong Courthouse, later home to Korea's Supreme Court for almost 50 years, in front of a modern gallery. Admission is free except for special exhibitions. It opens 10:00 to 20:00 from Tuesday to Thursday, to 21:00 on Fridays, and to 19:00 in summer or 18:00 in winter on weekends and holidays, and it closes on Mondays and January 1.

For a view down onto the palace roofs, the Jeong-dong Observatory is on the 13th floor of the Seoul City Hall Seosomun Building beside the palace; take elevator No. 3. The city lists it as open from 13:30 to 17:30 on weekdays and from 09:00 to 17:30 at weekends. The same city page lists a two-hour guided Jeong-dong walk that starts at the Deoksugung ticket booth and ends at Hwangudan (환구단), the imperial altar near City Hall.

en.heading: A walking order, from the 11:00 ceremony to dusk
paragraphs: This sequence fits Tuesday to Sunday and takes about four hours plus lunch. 10:45: arrive at Daehanmun from City Hall Station on Lines 1 and 2 and find a spot for the 11:00 guard ceremony. 11:30: buy a ticket, walk to Junghwajeon and the halls behind it, and register at Seokjojeon's information desk for the 11:50 English session, or for 14:50 if 11:50 is full. 12:45: Jeonggwanheon, then out through Daehanmun for lunch near City Hall.

14:00: walk the stone-wall road, step up to the Seoul Museum of Art for half an hour, then continue to the rotary and along Jeongdong-gil past the Methodist church and the Paichai building. 15:15: Jungmyeongjeon. 15:45: Jeong-dong Park and the Russian legation tower, then down Gojong's Road to the wall road. 16:30: on a weekday, go up to the Jeong-dong Observatory before it closes at 17:30 for the view back over the palace.

If you booked the 14:50 Seokjojeon session instead, swap the order: walk Jeong-dong in the late morning after the ceremony and return to the palace at 14:30. On a Monday the palace, the guard ceremony and the art museum are all off, so walk only the outside route and come back another day for the halls. In the evening Deoksugung is at its calmest, and its grounds stay open until 21:00.

faq.q: How long do I need for Deoksugung and Jeong-dong?
faq.a: About an hour for the palace grounds, 45 minutes for a Seokjojeon session and roughly two hours for the Jeong-dong walk with Jungmyeongjeon and the Russian legation tower. Four hours covers everything at a relaxed pace. With only one hour, walk the palace grounds and the stone-wall road.

faq.q: Can I visit Seokjojeon without booking ahead?
faq.a: Yes, on the English sessions at 11:50 and 14:50, which take foreign visitors first come at the museum's information desk, up to 20 people, with a passport or alien registration card. All other sessions need an online booking, which opens a week ahead. The hall is open from 09:30 to 17:30, with the last session at 16:30.

faq.q: Is the Deoksugung guard ceremony the same as Gyeongbokgung's?
faq.a: No. Deoksugung's ceremony is staged by the Seoul Metropolitan Government in front of Daehanmun at 11:00 and 14:00, every day except Monday, for about 25 minutes. Gyeongbokgung runs its own ceremony at different times; our five-palace comparison covers both. Either is free to watch, and weather can cancel them.

faq.q: Do couples really avoid the Deoksugung stone-wall road?
faq.a: Mostly as a joke. The saying that couples who walk it together will split up is usually traced to the family court that stood along the road and the Supreme Court above it, which couples passed on the way to divorce hearings. Plenty of couples walk it, especially in autumn.

faq.q: Can I visit Deoksugung in the evening?
faq.a: Yes. The grounds are open until 21:00, with last entry at 20:00, every day except Monday. Seokjojeon, Dondeokjeon and Jungmyeongjeon close at 17:30, so an evening visit is for the courtyards, Junghwajeon from outside and the stone-wall road, which is a public street.

guide.quickAnswer: Kimjang (김장) is the late-autumn making of a household's winter kimchi, shared between families and listed by UNESCO in 2013. Visitors are rarely part of a family kimjang, but Museum Kimchikan in Insadong runs one-hour English classes from Tuesday to Friday, making napa-cabbage kimchi in November and December. Carry any kimchi home in checked baggage, cold and double-bagged; in a carry-on it counts as a liquid.

en.heading: Kimjang: a winter's food supply, made and shared
paragraphs: In UNESCO's description, kimchi is vegetables preserved with seasonings and fermented seafood, and kimjang (김장, also spelled gimjang) is the communal job of making enough of it in late autumn to carry a household through the winter. UNESCO added 'Kimjang, making and sharing kimchi in the Republic of Korea' to its Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity in 2013. The word sharing in that title matters: the listing honors a social practice as much as a recipe.

The work runs all year. Households buy shrimp, anchovies and other seafood for salting in spring, sea salt for brine in summer and red chilies to dry and grind in late summer, then gather in late autumn on a day picked by watching the forecast. Relatives and neighbors help one another and swap finished kimchi, which spreads techniques between families. Recipes are treated as family heritage and, traditionally, passed from a mother-in-law to a newly married daughter-in-law.

On the day itself the work follows a set order. Whole cabbages are split and salted, often overnight, then rinsed and drained. Meanwhile the filling, 김칫소 (gimchitso), is mixed from radish strips, chili flakes, garlic, ginger, scallions and salted seafood. Everyone then sits around the pile, spreading filling between the leaves of each half cabbage and folding it into a tight bundle for the tub. Boiled pork eaten wrapped in fresh kimchi, bossam (보쌈), is the traditional reward at the end.

That defines a visitor's real position: kimjang is not a show. It happens in homes, apartment courtyards and community halls, among people who know one another, and nobody stages it for tourists. What you can do is notice its traces all over the city in November, learn the technique in a class and eat the results with some understanding of the work behind them, which is a fair way to meet it.

en.heading: Why November: a calendar set by the thermometer
paragraphs: Timing is about temperature. The Korea Meteorological Administration's rule of thumb is that kimjang suits the stretch when the daily low falls to 0°C or below and the daily mean stays at 4°C or below: cold enough for kimchi to ferment slowly through the winter, not yet cold enough for ingredients to freeze. In 2007, for example, the KMA advised Seoul households that the right moment would come around November 29, and warned that waiting too long risked a late-November cold snap freezing the cabbage and radish.

In practice the season now spreads across November, because many families store kimchi in dedicated kimchi refrigerators rather than in jars buried in the yard. You will see it in the shops: piles of napa cabbage and radish, sacks of chili flakes, garlic and tubs of salted shrimp. In 2025 Seoul's November kimjang event was built around a direct market selling exactly those ingredients to households.

There is also a date on the calendar. Since a 2020 amendment to the Kimchi Industry Promotion Act, November 22 has been Kimchi Day (김치의 날), set by law to promote the kimchi industry, pass on kimchi culture and tell the public about its nutritional value. The act lets national and local governments hold events, classes and campaigns around the day, so late November is when kimchi promotions cluster.

en.heading: The kimchi you will meet, and how to tell them apart
paragraphs: VisitKorea counts more than 100 kinds of kimchi, varying with region, climate and season, but a visitor meets the same handful again and again. These five are worth recognizing on menus, labels and side-dish plates. Kimjang itself is mostly about the first, made in quantity from whole heads of napa cabbage.

Two more words change how kimchi tastes. Fresh kimchi, 겉절이 (geotjeori), is dressed and eaten almost at once, crisp and bright. Long-fermented kimchi, 묵은지 (mugeunji), has been left for many months until it is sour and soft, and it gives the deepest kimchi stew. Kimjang kimchi moves from one state toward the other over the winter, which is why the same batch tastes different in December and in March.

If you avoid seafood, ask before you eat. Ordinary kimchi usually contains salted seafood, 젓갈 (jeotgal), which is part of the definition UNESCO uses. The question 젓갈 들어가요? (jeotgal deureogayo?, 'does it have salted seafood in it?') gets a straight answer, and white kimchi made without chili, 백김치 (baek-gimchi), is the gentlest choice if the heat is the problem.

en.heading: Museum Kimchikan: where to learn in English
paragraphs: Museum Kimchikan (뮤지엄김치간), run by the food company Pulmuone, fills the fourth to sixth floors of the Insadong Maru main building at 35-4 Insadong-gil. It is about ten minutes on foot from Jonggak Station Exit 3 on Line 1 or Anguk Station Exit 6 on Line 3. It opens from Tuesday to Sunday, 10:00 to 18:00, with last entry at 17:30, and closes on Mondays, January 1, December 25 and the three-day Seollal and Chuseok holidays.

Admission is 5,000 won for adults, 3,000 won for ages 8 to 18 and free for visitors 65 and over with ID. Individuals need no reservation. A free audio guide in English, Japanese and Chinese plays on your own phone after you scan a QR code, so bring earphones; the museum's docent tours are in Korean and only for booked groups of ten or more.

The classes are the reason to go in November. Kimchi! Basic, taught in English, runs from Tuesday to Friday at 10:00 and 14:00 for an hour, and in November and December it makes baechu-gimchi, the kimjang staple. It costs 40,000 won for adults, 38,000 won for ages 8 to 18 and 37,000 won for younger children, admission included. Kimchi All-in-one adds cooking with kimchi over 90 minutes, a cheese kimchi fried rice in this season, for 65,000 won, with at most 12 people.

Read the conditions before you book. A session needs at least four participants or it does not run, so a solo traveler should book early and keep the day flexible. Changes and cancellations close at 10:59 three days before the class; after that you pay for the places reserved, and late cancellers are barred from booking for six months. You must carry your kimchi out in the container and bag provided, because the museum does not ship.

en.heading: Is there a kimjang festival to join in 2026?
paragraphs: Probably not as a participant. Seoul's big November kimjang event has changed shape over the years. In 2025 the city co-hosted the Korea Kimjang Festival (대한민국 김장대축제) on Saturday, November 22, Kimchi Day, at the aT Center in Yangjae-dong. It had a kimchi culture exhibition, kimchi sales and a direct market for kimjang ingredients, and the city said kimchi-making was not offered to the general public because the space was too small.

As of October 25, 2026, neither Seoul nor its partners had announced a 2026 edition. If one is held, expect it close to Kimchi Day and expect details only shortly before; in 2025 the city's guide was posted days ahead. Check Seoul's news site, news.seoul.go.kr, in mid-November, but do not plan a trip around it, and treat any large kimjang event as a market and exhibition to browse rather than a class.

The dependable options are the scheduled ones: a Kimchikan class, which runs in English every week from Tuesday to Friday, and the National Folk Museum of Korea, whose hall on the Korean year sets kimjang beside the other winter tasks such as making fermented soybean blocks. Our folk museum guide explains that hall, and the museum sits inside Gyeongbokgung's grounds, so it pairs with a palace morning.

en.heading: Eating kimchi as a guest
paragraphs: At a Korean table, kimchi is part of the shared banchan (반찬), the side dishes, and refills are free. Ask for more by pointing at the dish and saying 이거 좀 더 주세요 (igeo jom deo juseyo). Take pieces from the side nearest you and do not turn the plate over hunting for the best leaf. Whole-leaf kimchi often arrives uncut; staff will cut it with scissors or hand them to you, which is normal rather than rude.

Restaurants must tell you where their kimchi comes from. Under Korea's origin-labeling rules, places that serve cabbage kimchi have to show the country of origin of both the cabbage and the chili powder, usually on a board by the counter or on the menu: 국산 or 국내산 means domestic, 중국산 means Chinese. Read the board if it matters to you, but there is no need to raise it at the table.

Compliments land well. Many restaurants make their own kimchi and take pride in it, and 김치 맛있어요 (gimchi masisseoyo, 'the kimchi is delicious') is the easiest way to please the cook. Do not leave a refilled dish untouched; take what you will eat. And if you are invited into a home in November, an offer to help carry or wash up will be appreciated far more than a request to film the kimjang.

en.heading: Buying kimchi to eat in Seoul
paragraphs: For eating during your stay, supermarkets and department-store food halls sell sealed tubs and pouches in sizes from a few hundred grams, and traditional markets sell kimchi by weight. Ask for 덜 익은 거 (deol igeun geo, less fermented) if you want it to keep, since it sours as it ages, or 잘 익은 거 (jal igeun geo, well fermented) if you want the tangy flavor now. Our Gwangjang Market guide explains how ordering at market counters works.

In November, the season is visible in the produce aisles even if you never buy an ingredient: stacked heads of cabbage, radishes with their greens on, and big bags of red pepper flakes. They show the scale of a household batch better than any museum label. If you have a hotel fridge, a small tub of baechu-gimchi and a packet of instant rice make a cheap breakfast with a sense of place.

Read the back of the pack as well as the front. Packaged kimchi lists its ingredients and the origin of the main ones, so you can check for 새우젓 (saeujeot, salted shrimp) or 멸치액젓 (myeolchi aekjeot, anchovy sauce) if you avoid seafood. Small packs suit a short stay better than a bargain kilo: once opened, kimchi keeps souring in the fridge, and the smell travels to everything around it.

en.heading: Taking kimchi home: gas, cold and airport security
paragraphs: Kimchi keeps fermenting after you buy it, and fermentation makes gas. A Korea Food Research Institute study of packaged kimchi found that packs began to swell after about 40 hours at 20°C and burst on the third day; at 10°C they swelled after about five days and burst on day eight; at 0°C they took about 30 days to swell and did not burst. The lesson: keep it cold until the last moment and expect the pack to puff.

Pack it in checked baggage. Incheon Airport treats kimchi in a carry-on as a liquid, allowed only in containers of 100 milliliters or less that fit in a single one-liter plastic bag, and it confiscated 10.7 tons of kimchi at security in 2024. Put a factory-sealed pack inside two zip bags with room to swell, wrap it in clothing in the middle of the suitcase and buy it the day before you fly. Check your destination's food-import rules as well.

Kimchi you make in a class comes in a container meant for the trip back to your hotel, not for a long flight. Refrigerate it as soon as you can and eat it during your stay; for the journey home, buy a commercially sealed pack instead.

en.heading: A November afternoon built around kimchi
paragraphs: Here is how a Wednesday in mid-November can run. 13:30: reach Insadong and walk up Insadong-gil to the Insadong Maru building; search 뮤지엄김치간 in Naver Map or Kakao Map. 14:00: the Kimchi! Basic class, booked at least a few days ahead, making baechu-gimchi. 15:00: the exhibition floors with the English audio guide on your phone. 16:30: drop your kimchi in the hotel fridge. 18:30: dinner of kimchi-jjigae, or bossam, boiled pork wrapped in fresh kimchi, the dish many families eat on kimjang day itself.

Run through these points before you book a class. They cover nearly every way a kimchi plan goes wrong for visitors, from a session cancelled for lack of numbers to a tub of fresh kimchi with nowhere cold to go, and none of them takes more than a minute to check.

Bring your phone and earphones for the free English audio guide.
Mention allergies when you book; kimchi usually contains salted seafood.
Avoid Mondays and the Seollal and Chuseok holidays, when the museum is closed.

faq.q: Can tourists join a family kimjang in Seoul?
faq.a: Rarely. Kimjang is a household and community event among people who know one another, and it is not staged for visitors. The practical way to take part is a class: Museum Kimchikan in Insadong teaches Kimchi! Basic in English from Tuesday to Friday, making napa-cabbage kimchi in November and December. In 2025 the city's November kimjang event offered no public kimchi-making.

faq.q: Do I need to book a kimchi-making class in advance?
faq.a: Yes. Museum Kimchikan's classes are booked online and need at least four participants to run, so book a few days ahead and keep the date flexible if you are traveling alone. Changes and cancellations close at 10:59 three days before; after that you pay for the places reserved. Museum entry without a class needs no booking.

faq.q: Can I take kimchi on a plane from Korea?
faq.a: In checked baggage, yes, well sealed. In a carry-on, Incheon Airport treats kimchi as a liquid, so only containers of 100 milliliters or less in a one-liter bag pass security. Use a factory-sealed pack, double-bag it and leave room for it to swell, because fermentation continues. Check your destination's food-import rules too.

faq.q: Is kimchi vegetarian?
faq.a: Usually not. Ordinary kimchi is seasoned with salted seafood such as shrimp or anchovy, which is part of how UNESCO's kimjang listing describes it. Ask 젓갈 들어가요? (jeotgal deureogayo?) before eating, and look for temple-food restaurants or white kimchi, baek-gimchi, if you need a version without seafood or chili.

faq.q: When is Kimchi Day?
faq.a: November 22. It was written into the Kimchi Industry Promotion Act in 2020 to promote kimchi culture and its nutritional value, and governments may hold events around it. In 2025 Seoul co-hosted the Korea Kimjang Festival on that day at the aT Center; no 2026 date had been announced by late October.

title.en: Changgyeonggung Palace Guide: The Queens' Palace, Zoo Years and Evenings

summary.en: Changgyeonggung explained: the 1483 palace for widowed queens, its oldest throne hall, the zoo era and 1909 greenhouse, evening hours, and the walk to Jongmyo.

guide.audience: Visitors seeing Changdeokgung or Jongmyo who want to know whether Changgyeonggung is worth adding, what its buildings mean and how to use its long evening hours.

guide.quickAnswer: Changgyeonggung (창경궁) is the quiet palace beside Changdeokgung: enlarged in 1483 for three widowed queens, turned into a zoo and botanical garden under Japanese rule, and restored from 1983. It has the oldest surviving throne hall of any Joseon palace and a 1909 glasshouse, costs 1,000 won, closes on Mondays and stays open until 21:00.

en.heading: A palace built for three widowed queens
paragraphs: Changgyeonggung (창경궁) began as a home for a retired king. In 1418, the year King Sejong took the throne, he built Suganggung (수강궁) on this hill for his father, King Taejong, who had abdicated in his favor. In 1483 King Seongjong enlarged it for three senior women of the royal family, his grandmother, his mother and his aunt, all of them widowed queens, and renamed it Changgyeonggung. With Changdeokgung next door it formed a single royal compound known as Donggwol (동궐), the East Palace.

That origin explains what you see. Changgyeonggung was a palace to live in rather than a stage for government, so its halls are lower and more domestic than Gyeongbokgung's, and its grounds open out into woods and a pond instead of running along a ceremonial axis. Its record is one of repeated loss and rebuilding: everything burned in the 1592 Japanese invasion, the inner quarters burned again in Yi Gwal's rebellion of 1624 and were rebuilt from 1633, and a great fire in 1830 destroyed most of the buildings, which were rebuilt by 1834.

Royal family history runs close to the surface here. Crown Prince Sado, son of King Yeongjo, was born in the palace's Jipbokheon (집복헌) hall in 1735. In the summer of 1762 Yeongjo summoned him to the courtyard of Munjeongjeon (문정전), then serving as a memorial hall for the late queen, and had him sealed in a wooden rice chest, where he died eight days later. Munjeongjeon still stands beside the throne hall, rebuilt in the 1980s, and knowing the story changes how its plain courtyard feels.

en.heading: Myeongjeongjeon: the oldest throne hall, facing east
paragraphs: From the main gate, Honghwamun (홍화문), you cross the arched stone bridge Okcheongyo (옥천교) and pass through Myeongjeongmun to reach Myeongjeongjeon (명정전), the throne hall. It was first built in 1484, burned in 1592 and rebuilt in 1616 under King Gwanghaegun, and it has come through every fire since. Its sturdy bracket work once led scholars to date it to the early Joseon period, until an ink inscription found inside the gable in 1963, matching the royal annals, settled the 1616 date. It is the oldest main hall of any Joseon palace and a National Treasure.

Set it beside Gyeongbokgung's Geunjeongjeon or Changdeokgung's Injeongjeon and two differences stand out. It is a single-story hall five bays wide rather than a towering two-story one, and it faces east rather than south. The Encyclopedia of Korean Culture ties both features to the palace's purpose: it was built as a residence for queen dowagers, not as the seat from which a king governed. Honghwamun and Myeongjeongmun belong to the same early 17th-century rebuilding, which makes this gate-and-hall sequence one of the oldest groups of wooden palace architecture in Seoul.

Take a few minutes in the courtyard. Twenty-four rank stones (품계석) line the raised royal path, marking where officials stood by grade for New Year greetings, state ceremonies and the reception of foreign envoys. The hall stands on a two-tier stone platform about 2.5 meters high. Look up at the dense clusters of brackets under the eaves, and through the doorway for the throne, the screen of the sun, moon and five peaks behind it, and the pair of carved phoenixes set into the ceiling above.

en.heading: From palace to Changgyeongwon: the zoo and garden years
paragraphs: The decline began in 1907, the year Emperor Sunjong came to the throne under Japanese control. From 1908 most of the palace's buildings were demolished or altered, and in 1909 a zoo and a botanical garden opened on the grounds, with Sunjong attending the opening ceremony. A museum went up on the cleared ground around the throne hall. In 1911 the palace was formally demoted to a public park and renamed Changgyeongwon (창경원), the final syllable meaning a garden rather than a palace.

Thousands of cherry trees, a symbol of Japan, were planted across the grounds, and from April 1924 the colonial authorities opened them for night blossom viewing. A Japanese-style pavilion was built beside the pond. In the early 1930s a road, today's Yulgok-ro, was cut through the ground linking the palace to Jongmyo, the royal ancestral shrine. The amusement-park identity outlived colonial rule: the National Archives of Korea records dense crowds in April 1971 and 918 children reported lost during the 1972 blossom season.

Restoration came late. In 1983 the government announced a plan, closed the grounds for two years and restored the name Changgyeonggung. The animals moved to the new Seoul Grand Park in Gwacheon, south of the city, and most of the cherry trees were transplanted, many of them to Yunjungno on Yeouido, with pines and zelkovas planted in their place. The rebuilding was completed on August 23, 1986. For Koreans who grew up before 1983, Changgyeongwon was simply the city zoo, which is why you may still hear the old name.

en.heading: Daeonsil, the glasshouse with a double meaning
paragraphs: The white glasshouse north of the halls is Daeonsil (대온실), the Great Greenhouse, completed in 1909 as Korea's first Western-style greenhouse. It was designed by Fukuba Hayato, head of the Japanese imperial gardens, and built by a French company. Fukuba had worked at Shinjuku Gyoen in Tokyo, whose 1896 greenhouse was Japan's first, and the two buildings are strikingly alike. A frame of cast iron and timber carries the glass above a granite base, 33 meters long and 10.5 meters high, which still looks light for its size.

Its history is not innocent. The Encyclopedia of Korean Culture describes the greenhouse and the zoo as built on the pretext of consoling Sunjong after Japan had confined him to Changdeokgung, and it reads the glasshouse as both an advanced piece of modern architecture and an instrument for erasing a Joseon palace. Tropical plants under iron and glass were the prestige display of empires at the time. The building survived damage in the Korean War, was registered as national heritage on February 6, 2004, and reopened in November 2017 after 15 months of restoration.

Our advice is to visit it for both reasons. The white tracery and the plants make it the most photographed spot in the palace, and its story makes it the most instructive. After dark the greenhouse area is part of the evening zone. The palace keeps the interior open in the evening in November and from March to October, but from December to February it closes the inside at 18:00 to protect the plants, so a winter evening visit means viewing it from outside.

en.heading: Chundangji pond, Tongmyeongjeon and the fenced-off corner
paragraphs: Chundangji (춘당지), the pond in the northern half of the grounds, belongs to the same colonial chapter. According to the Encyclopedia of Korean Culture, it was dug in front of the Chundangdae terrace as part of the garden works, with a Japanese-style water pavilion built to its north. Today it is the calmest corner of the palace, ringed by old trees that turn red and gold from late October into November, and it needs no booking, which makes it a good substitute on days when the Changdeokgung Secret Garden is sold out.

Two notices affect this side of the palace in 2026. Since February 10, part of the path around the pond has been closed from 18:00 to 21:00 until its lighting is repaired. Since September 22, 2025, most of Gwollae Gaksa (궐내각사), the area of former government offices on the palace's south side, has been fenced off while the royal stables are reconstructed. You can still reach Seoninmun gate, the stone observatory platform Gwancheondae (관천대) and the Yulgok-ro gate.

Between the throne hall and the pond, look for Tongmyeongjeon (통명전), a royal sleeping hall rebuilt after the fire of 1830, with a stone-lined pool beside it. It stays inside the evening zone, so you can leave it until after dark. The palace's open halls in 2026, by day and by night, are Yanghwadang, Tongmyeongjeon, Gyeongchunjeon, Haminjeong, Hwangyeongjeon, Munjeongjeon and Myeongjeongjeon, plus the greenhouse and the pond.

en.heading: Hours, tickets and the evening switch
paragraphs: Changgyeonggung keeps the simplest timetable of the palaces: 09:00 to 21:00 every day of the year except Monday, with last entry at 20:00. When a Monday is a public holiday the palace opens and closes on the next non-holiday instead. Adults pay 1,000 won, which for foreign visitors means ages 19 to 64. Foreign visitors 18 and under or 65 and over enter free, as does anyone wearing hanbok, and every Wednesday is a free Culture Day. The 6,000-won integrated pass also covers it.

The whole palace does not stay open after dark. At a set time each evening, shown in the table, staff move everyone into an evening zone built around five areas: Honghwamun, Myeongjeongjeon, Tongmyeongjeon, Chundangji and the greenhouse. Anything outside them, such as the wooded paths and the outer corners near Gwancheondae, is a daytime sight, so if you arrive in the afternoon, walk those first. The same table gives the last entry through the Yulgok-ro gate from Jongmyo, which follows a different clock.

Two 2026 dates matter. From October 29 to November 15, admission is free for everyone during the Korea Grand Festival, with Mondays still closed. From November 10 to 15, the regular evening opening is suspended for Donggwol Dongnak (동궐동락), a separately booked night program; on those days the palace closes at 17:30, with last entry at 16:30. Booking details are announced on the Royal Palaces and Tombs Center notice board, and enquiries go to 1522-2295.

Search 창경궁 in Naver Map or Kakao Map. Hyehwa Station Exit 4 on Line 4 is about 12 minutes on foot from the main gate, and several city buses stop at 창경궁·서울대학교병원. The palace's car park is closed until December 31, 2026, so come by public transport. The palace office is on 02-762-4868.

en.heading: Walking on to Jongmyo over the buried road
paragraphs: For most of the 20th century the palace and Jongmyo were split by the road cut in the early 1930s, crossed only by a footbridge, Gwandeokgyo, that was later removed. Seoul's restoration project, begun about 2010 and finished in 2022, put that stretch of Yulgok-ro into a tunnel, laid about 8,000 square meters of green space over it, rebuilt 503 meters of palace wall on its old line and restored Buksinmun (북신문), the north gate through which kings entered the shrine informally. A 340-meter path along the wall opened on July 22, 2022.

The path opened before the gates did. In 2022 it led into neither site, and the city said it was still negotiating access with the heritage authorities. Today the Yulgok-ro gate into Changgyeonggung and Buksinmun into Jongmyo open on Saturdays, Sundays, public holidays and Culture Day. Admission is now free every Wednesday, but the palace's hours page still lists its Yulgok-ro gate for the last Wednesday of the month only, so on other Wednesdays confirm at the gate. Each site needs its own ticket, so keep some cash or a card ready at both ends.

Direction matters. Jongmyo closes earlier, at 17:30 from November to January with last entry at 16:30, while Changgyeonggung stays open until 21:00, so on a winter weekend see the shrine first and enter the palace through the Yulgok-ro gate before 17:00. On the west side, Hamyangmun (함양문) links Changgyeonggung with Changdeokgung's palace halls, though not with its Secret Garden. You buy the next ticket at the gate, and crossings stop at Changdeokgung's last entry, 16:30 from November to January.

en.heading: A Saturday plan, and who should skip the palace
paragraphs: A November Saturday, about four and a half hours: at 14:30, enter Jongmyo from Jongno 3-ga Station Exit 11, five minutes away, and walk past its two great halls, since weekends there are self-guided. At 15:45, leave by Buksinmun, follow the wall path and enter Changgyeonggung by the Yulgok-ro gate. At 16:00, see Gwancheondae, then Munjeongjeon and Myeongjeongjeon in the low sun, and walk the wooded paths before the 17:30 switch to the evening zone. After that, Tongmyeongjeon, the greenhouse, which stays open inside on November evenings, and a circuit of Chundangji. Return to the lit throne hall and leave by Honghwamun around 19:00 for dinner near Hyehwa. On November 10 to 15, 2026, drop the evening part.

Who should come? Anyone on a second palace day, anyone who wants an evening among historic buildings after the other palaces have closed, autumn visitors who could not get a Secret Garden ticket, and readers interested in the colonial period, which is easier to read here than at most palaces. An hour covers the main sights, ninety minutes with the greenhouse and pond. Skip it on a first trip with only one palace slot, when Gyeongbokgung or Changdeokgung will give you more, and do not come for pageantry: there is no guard ceremony.

Three mistakes are common. Visitors arrive at 18:00 expecting the whole palace and find only the evening zone open; they plan the Jongmyo link on a weekday when the gates are shut; or they assume Hamyangmun leads into the Secret Garden. Check the day of the week, the month and the notice board, in that order, and the palace is easy.

faq.q: Is Changgyeonggung worth visiting if I have already seen Changdeokgung?
faq.a: Yes, if you have an extra hour. It adds the oldest surviving throne hall of any Joseon palace, the 1909 glasshouse, a large pond and a clear view of what colonial rule did to Seoul's palaces. Walk in through Hamyangmun gate before Changdeokgung's last entry, buying the 1,000-won ticket at the gate.

faq.q: Can I go inside the greenhouse in the evening?
faq.a: In November and from March to October, yes: the interior stays open as part of the evening zone. From December to February the palace closes the inside at 18:00 to protect the plants, so after that you see it lit from outside only. Daytime visits are possible all year.

faq.q: What happened to the Changgyeongwon zoo?
faq.a: It closed when the restoration plan was announced in 1983. The animals were moved to the new Seoul Grand Park in Gwacheon, most of the cherry trees were transplanted, and the palace's name was restored. Rebuilding work was completed in August 1986.

faq.q: Is there a bridge between Changgyeonggung and Jongmyo?
faq.a: No. The road that separated them, Yulgok-ro, now runs through a tunnel with green space and a wall path above it. Gates on that path open on Saturdays, Sundays, public holidays and Culture Day, and each site needs its own ticket.

faq.q: Do I need to book anything?
faq.a: Not for ordinary daytime or evening visits; buy a ticket at the gate. Only special programs need booking, such as Donggwol Dongnak, the night program that replaces the regular evening opening from November 10 to 15, 2026.

summary.en: Namdaemun, Gwangjang, Tongin, Mangwon, Gyeongdong and Dongdaemun's fabric market compared: what each is best for, hours, Sunday closures, payment and manners.

guide.audience: Independent visitors who want one or two traditional markets in a Seoul trip and need to choose between them, then shop, eat and pay without confusion.
guide.method: Researched from the official sources listed below, checked on October 25, 2026. Hours, fees and booking rules can change; the linked official pages are the final word.
guide.quickAnswer: For street food, go to Gwangjang, whose food alley runs until 23:00. For a calm first market, try Tongin near Gyeongbokgung; for everyday neighborhood life, Mangwon; for herbs and ginseng, Gyeongdong; for kitchenware and wholesale goods, Namdaemun; for fabric and craft supplies, the Dongdaemun Shopping Complex. Namdaemun and Dongdaemun close on Sundays, so carry small notes and check the day first.

en.heading: What makes a sijang different from a supermarket
paragraphs: A traditional market, 전통시장 (jeontong sijang), is not one store but a district of independent stalls and small shops, often under a shared arcade roof, each run by its own owner on its own schedule. That is why the first rule for any market is to check the stall, not the market: the published hours tell you when the lanes are open, not whether a particular counter is. Seoul's markets range from wholesale districts six centuries old to neighborhood food lanes, and the right one depends on what you want to do there.

Seoul has had markets for as long as it has been a capital. Namdaemun Market traces its beginning to 1414, when the Joseon government leased shops near the city's south gate to merchants, and in 1897 it became Seoul's first modern permanent market. Gyeongdong opened in 1960 as a market for farm produce and grew, after its main building was finished in 1985, into Korea's largest ginseng and herbal-medicine quarter. Mangwon has served its riverside neighborhood for more than forty years.

Markets are also changing under pressure. The culture ministry calls overcharging and unfriendly service the biggest obstacles to domestic tourism, and since 2023 it and the Korea Tourism Organization have been selecting K-Tourism Markets (케이-관광마켓) for two years of support. In May 2026 they named eleven for the second round, including Mangwon and Gyeongdong in Seoul, and merchants from all eleven signed a pledge on four points: fixed, posted prices; card payment; cleanliness; and courtesy. Treat that pledge as the standard to expect anywhere.

en.heading: Six markets at a glance
paragraphs: The table gives each market's strength and timetable, using hours published by the market itself or by the city and national tourism sites, Visit Seoul and VisitKorea. Individual stalls open later and close earlier as they please, and markets post their own closures around Seollal and Chuseok. When a particular shop matters, look it up in Naver Map or Kakao Map by its Korean name the evening before, and use the subway exit in the last column as your meeting point rather than a street address.

If you have time for only one, let the purpose decide. Eating is Gwangjang's job, gifts with a story are Gyeongdong's, and a sense of how Seoul households shop is Mangwon's. Namdaemun rewards a buyer with a list, the Dongdaemun Shopping Complex a maker with a project, and Tongin a visitor with an hour to spare near the palaces. Trying to see three markets in a morning mostly shows you the same plastic awnings three times; one market done slowly, with a meal in it, is the better trip.

en.heading: Namdaemun: six centuries of buying wholesale
paragraphs: Namdaemun Market (남대문시장) spreads over about 66,000 square meters below Sungnyemun, the old south gate, with about 10,172 shops selling some 1,700 kinds of goods to roughly 300,000 visitors a day, by the market's own count. Visit Seoul calls it the largest traditional market in Korea. It is a wholesale market first: shops are small, many deal in goods made by their owners or their suppliers, and retailers from across the country buy here at night, leaving the daytime to local shoppers and tourists.

The market's own directory doubles as a shopping list: clothing and fashion goods, accessories, children's clothes, wedding goods and kitchenware, imported food and stationery, farm and fishery products with ginseng, flowers and crafts, and jewelry, watches and cameras. For visitors the most rewarding are the kitchenware arcades, the children's clothing wholesalers and the ginseng shops, where buying wholesale means prices are worth comparing across several neighboring stalls before you commit.

Food is part of the trip, and the market names its own specialties: long-established oxtail-soup restaurants, a braised cutlassfish alley (갈치골목, galchi golmok), a knife-cut noodle alley (칼국수골목, kalguksu golmok), vegetable-filled hotteok, chicken soup and a North Korean-style cold-noodle house. Our street-food guide explains how to find the kalguksu alley's easy-to-miss door.

Go Monday to Saturday between mid-morning and mid-afternoon; most shops close on Sunday, and each arcade keeps its own hours. Hoehyeon Station on Line 4 has three exits, 5, 6 and 7, that put you in the market within about five minutes, and Sungnyemun, Deoksugung, Myeong-dong and the foot of Namsan are all within walking distance, which makes Namdaemun the easiest market to fold into a central-Seoul day.

en.heading: Gwangjang and the fabric floors of Dongdaemun
paragraphs: Gwangjang Market (광장시장), at Jongno 5-ga, is the market to choose for food. Its central alley of counter stalls serves mung-bean pancakes, mayak gimbap and knife-cut noodles from 09:00 to 23:00 all year, Sundays included, while the silk, bedding and hanbok shops around it trade from 09:00 to 18:00 and close on Sundays, as does the secondhand clothing arcade, open 10:00 to 19:00. Our Gwangjang guide covers ordering at the counters, prices and the market's overcharging controversies in detail.

A short walk east along Jongno, beside Heunginjimun, the great East Gate, the Dongdaemun Shopping Complex (동대문종합시장) is a supply market: you come here for materials, not finished clothes. Its fabric and garment-material floors open 08:00 to 18:00, the accessory-parts floors 09:30 to 19:00, and the bedding, embroidery, curtain and tableware floors 08:00 to 19:00. The whole complex closes on Sundays, except that some home-goods shops open on the first, third and fifth Sundays. Dongdaemun Station Exit 9, on Lines 1 and 4, connects to it underground.

If you do not sew, give it fifteen minutes between Gwangjang and the East Gate, mainly to see a working wholesale building in full swing. If you do, come early on a weekday, bring photos or samples of what you are making, and plan on a morning; the building is large, the shops are specialized, and the fabric floors close at 18:00.

en.heading: Gyeongdong and Seoul Yangnyeongsi: the herbal quarter
paragraphs: In Jegi-dong, in Seoul's northeast, two markets run into each other. Gyeongdong Market (경동시장) opened in June 1960 as a market for farm produce; after the Gyeongdong Building was completed in 1985 it grew into Korea's largest ginseng and herbal-medicine quarter. Seoul Yangnyeongsi (서울약령시), the herbal market beside it, began in the late 1960s with a few herb shops and now has more than 800 herbal shops and clinics, through which, Visit Seoul says, about 70 percent of the herbal medicine traded in Korea passes.

Walk in from Jegi-dong Station Exit 2 and you are among open sacks of dried roots, bark, berries and flowers, each labeled by hand in Korean, alongside ginseng in several forms, dried jujubes and milk-vetch root. You do not need to want medicine to enjoy it. Packaged jujubes or ginseng make good gifts, but check your home country's rules on importing plant products before buying loose roots or seeds, and do not take a remedy on a vendor's word: Korean medicine is prescribed by licensed doctors (한의사, hanuisa) at the clinics around the market.

Gyeongdong posts hours of 08:00 to 18:00 every day but closes every other Sunday and over Chuseok; the herbal market keeps about 09:00 to 18:00, varying by shop, and its herb medicine museum across the street closes on Mondays. Visit Seoul's listing points hungry visitors to a mugwort rice-cake shop nearby and to Cheongnyangni's chicken alley a few minutes' walk away. Gyeongdong lies off the usual sightseeing circuit, but Line 1 runs straight there from Jongno, and it is one of Seoul's two K-Tourism Markets in the 2026 round.

en.heading: Mangwon: the neighborhood market young Seoul adopted
paragraphs: Mangwon Market (망원시장), near the Han River in Mapo-gu, is the opposite of a tourist market. It has served Mangwon-dong for more than forty years under a 215-meter arcade with public restrooms and a public car park, and it sells what a neighborhood needs: vegetables, fruit, meat, fish, rice cakes, tofu and household goods. What changed is the crowd. The market itself says that, together with the café street Mangridan-gil nearby, it has become a favorite of Seoul's twenty- and thirty-somethings for cheap snacks and fresh food.

Its official store directory lists the counters people come for, from hotteok and mini gimbap to jeon and jokbal, braised pig's trotters. The merchants run a Bring Your Own Container campaign, so a lunch box or tote bag in your daypack is welcome, and the market's own pages list stalls by type, from produce and meat to seafood, restaurants and processed foods such as tofu. In 2026 the government picked Mangwon as one of Seoul's two K-Tourism Markets, and its merchants signed the pledge on posted prices and card payment.

Mangwon is the market for a slow afternoon. From Mangwon Station Exit 2 on Line 6 it is a five-minute walk. Buy picnic food, then carry on to Mangwon Hangang Park on the riverbank; the 2026 K-Tourism Market launch at Mangwon trialed exactly that route as a tour package, shopping at the market followed by a picnic by the Han. There is no single market timetable, since each shop sets its own hours, so check any stall you are set on in Naver Map. It is weaker for souvenirs than Namdaemun and less of a show than Gwangjang, which is the point.

en.heading: Tongin: the gentlest first market
paragraphs: With one free hour near Gyeongbokgung, Tongin Market (통인시장) is the easiest introduction. It opened in 1941 as a public market for Japanese residents and now has more than seventy food stalls and grocers along a single covered lane, about 500 meters from Gyeongbokgung Station Exit 2, open 07:00 to 21:00 depending on the shop. It is best known for its dosirak café, where you buy old-style coins, yeopjeon (엽전), and trade them at stalls along the lane for small portions to fill a lunch tray.

The café keeps shorter hours than the lane, 11:00 to 15:00 on weekdays and to 16:00 at weekends, and Visit Seoul lists it as closed on Mondays and the third Sunday of the month; our Seochon guide explains the token system and a conflicting report about its weekly closing day. Try the gireum tteokbokki, rice cakes stir-fried in oil and chili. Pair Tongin with Gyeongbokgung in the morning or with a Seochon walk; it is too small to justify a special trip across the city.

en.heading: Paying, bargaining and market manners
paragraphs: Cash still matters. Many stalls take cards, and the K-Tourism pledge pushes more of them to, but some counters still prefer cash, so carry 1,000-, 5,000- and 10,000-won notes and ask 카드 돼요? (kadeu dwaeyo?, 'do you take cards?') before you order. If a vendor asks for a bank transfer, pay in cash instead, since a transfer needs a Korean bank account. Find the posted price before food is served, or ask 얼마예요? (eolmayeyo?, 'how much is it?'), and repeat the number back if you are unsure.

Bargaining is narrower than many visitors expect. Food, produce and anything with a posted price is not negotiable, and haggling over a small snack is pointless and unwelcome. In clothing and souvenir shops, especially when you buy several items, a polite 조금만 깎아 주세요 (jogeumman kkakka juseyo, 'a little discount, please') may earn a small reduction; do not push. A vendor may instead add a little extra, deom (덤), the market's own form of goodwill, which you accept with thanks.

Market lanes are workplaces. Ask before photographing a vendor or a stall up close, do not squeeze fruit or open packages without asking, and step aside to read your phone rather than stopping in a narrow aisle where carts and delivery scooters pass. Eat at the counter or seating area where you bought the food instead of walking through crowds with it. Before you set out, run through this list.
checklist: Check the day: Sundays close Namdaemun, the Dongdaemun Shopping Complex and Gwangjang's shops, and Gyeongdong closes every other Sunday.
Carry small notes, and ask 카드 돼요? before ordering if you want to pay by card.
Find a posted price, or agree the price before anything is served or wrapped.
Bring a tote bag or a container, especially for Mangwon's container campaign.
Ask before taking close-up photos of vendors and their stalls.
Turn down any request for a bank transfer and pay by cash or card.

en.heading: Two market days, east and west
paragraphs: An east-side weekday on Line 1, about six hours: at 09:30, leave Jegi-dong Station by Exit 2 into the herbal market as shops open, and buy jujubes or ginseng tea. At 11:15, ride Line 1 four stops west to Jongno 5-ga; Gwangjang's food alley is easiest before the lunch rush. At 13:30, walk east along Jongno to the Dongdaemun Shopping Complex for half an hour among the fabric floors, then step out to Heunginjimun and either climb the Naksan section of the city wall or follow Cheonggyecheon back west as the light fades.

A west-side day: Tongin with Gyeongbokgung in the morning, then west across the city to Mangwon for a late lunch and a picnic by the Han, finishing in the cafés of Mangridan-gil. Save Namdaemun for a weekday morning with Deoksugung or Myeong-dong. On a Sunday, keep to Gwangjang's food alley, which VisitKorea lists as open all year, and to any stalls you have confirmed in a map app, and leave the wholesale markets for another day.

faq.q: Which Seoul market is best for street food?
faq.a: Gwangjang, whose central food alley of counter stalls stays open until 23:00, including Sundays, when the surrounding shops are closed. Tongin near Gyeongbokgung is calmer, with its coin lunchbox, and Mangwon has neighborhood snack counters. Our Gwangjang guide explains how ordering at the counters works.

faq.q: Are Seoul's traditional markets open on Sundays?
faq.a: Some are. Gwangjang's food alley opens on Sundays, but its shops, Namdaemun and the Dongdaemun Shopping Complex close. Gyeongdong closes every other Sunday, and Tongin and Mangwon vary shop by shop. On a Sunday, choose food over shopping and confirm individual stalls in Naver Map or Kakao Map.

faq.q: Can I pay by card at traditional markets?
faq.a: Often, but not everywhere. Many shops and stalls take cards, and the markets in the government's K-Tourism Market program, including Mangwon and Gyeongdong, have pledged card payment. Carry small notes anyway, ask 카드 돼요? before ordering, and pay cash rather than agreeing to a bank transfer.

faq.q: Is bargaining expected in Seoul's markets?
faq.a: Not for food, produce or anything with a posted price. In clothing and souvenir shops, a polite request for a small discount may work when you buy several items, but do not push. Some vendors add a little extra, called deom, instead of cutting the price.

faq.q: Where can I buy ginseng or herbal teas?
faq.a: Gyeongdong Market and the Seoul Yangnyeongsi herbal market beside it, near Jegi-dong Station on Line 1, have the widest choice, and Namdaemun has ginseng shops in the center. Packaged products are the easiest to take home; check your country's import rules for plant products first.

guide.quickAnswer: Seoul has two lantern festivals. The Seoul Lantern Festival (서울빛초롱축제) is a free, city-run walk past lit sculptures along Cheonggyecheon stream; Seoul's festival calendar lists the 2026 edition for December, but exact dates had not been announced by October 25, 2026.
